correctness.rationale: A blue vertex in a layer with u whites has u white clique neighbors plus its mate if white. A full layer can force every missing mate; two incomplete layers with at least two whites each are stuck. With just one white a_j on one side and at least two on the other, a first force exists exactly when some initially blue b_i has i!=j, and that force fills all of A. With one white on each side, n>=3 gives a blue matched pair avoiding both white indices. Counting the disjoint regimes gives each term (subtract the duplicate all-blue set; the boundary with only one blue on the sparse side contributes 2n(n-1)z^n). The minimum sets are the full layers and the indicated near-layer sets, and every successful set contains one by keeping a full layer or just one usable mate in the sparse side. At n=3 the interior sum vanishes and the coefficients in degrees 3,4,5,6 are 14,15,6,1. Summing the general coefficients gives 2(n+1)2^n-n^2-6n-1; division by 4^n gives the uniform probability. The bundled bounded script was inspected, not run; no finite census is needed for the proof.

evidence: The rook-graph criterion is a forest with an isolated row and a column leaf or an isolated column and a row leaf (plus the empty-edge case); there is a full polynomial for all dimensions. Pelayo–Abara give a maximum failed-set size, fort/fractional work gives other product parameters, and Grood et al. characterize well-forced trees.

evidence: White cells are edges, so the two row degrees are u,v; an isolated column is an index blue in both layers, and a row leaf means exactly one white vertex in its layer.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: If a row is empty of whites, all nonisolated columns are leaves. Otherwise criterion success requires a row leaf and an isolated column; a forest is then automatic, as every two-row cycle needs both rows with at least two edges. For u=v=1 an isolated column exists for n>=3; for u=1, v>=2 it exists exactly when a blue b_i avoids the unique white index in A. Choosing the singleton and the other white set directly expands the all-coefficient count into the frozen polynomial. Every resulting white set can be enlarged either by filling the other row when one row is empty, or by filling all positions of the other row except one preserved empty column when there is a singleton row. This gives a containing successful white set of size n and proves well-forcedness immediately from the known criterion. The total and random probability are evaluations of the enumerator.
